analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to pay landowners when environmental rules cut their property value by half or more.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 1996 with 35 Senate backers, the bill sat on the Senate calendar and never received a committee hearing or floor vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a sweeping new right to taxpayer compensation for property owners affected by federal regulation. Any federal action that cut a property's value by 50% or more would trigger a payment from the regulating agency's budget, and landowners facing wetlands or endangered species restrictions would get new administrative appeals, compensation offers, and binding arbitration. It would also have required agencies to write a 'taking impact analysis' before issuing rules likely to burden property, and to get written consent before entering private land to collect data.
analysis.who_benefits: Private landowners whose property value falls sharply because of federal rules — most often owners of large tracts affected by wetlands and endangered species restrictions, such as developers, farmers, and timber, mining, and energy interests. Smaller landowners would gain procedural rights too: a say in agency data collection, administrative appeals, and attorney fees if they win in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large landowners, developers, and resource extractors

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal claim requiring compensation whenever agency action deprives an owner of 50% or more of a property's value, with the government bearing the burden of proof in most cases [S3].
Lets property owners file both money and injunction claims in a single court of their choice, ending the old split between district courts and the Court of Federal Claims [S3].

Gives landowners new administrative appeal rights over wetlands permits and endangered species decisions, and lets them choose between selling their land to the agency at unrestricted value or being paid the difference [S2, S3].
Bars federal officials from entering private property to collect data without written consent and from using that data against the owner without a chance to dispute it [S2, S3].
Requires federal agencies to publish a written 'taking impact analysis' estimating compensation liability before issuing rules likely to take property [S2, S3].
Awards court costs and attorney fees to any property owner who prevails against the government [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, because every compensation award and arbitration payment would come out of the regulated agency's own operating appropriations. The public also bears the indirect cost: agencies facing liability for every significant habitat or wetlands restriction would have strong reason to issue fewer of them, weakening protections that benefit everyone.

drawbacks.text: Paying compensation out of each agency's operating budget would make enforcing the Endangered Species Act and Clean Water Act wetlands rules far more expensive, giving agencies a direct financial incentive to decline to restrict damaging land use [S3].

The 50%-of-value compensation trigger and expanded definitions of a taking go well beyond what courts then required under the Fifth Amendment, converting many ordinary permit conditions and habitat rules into payable claims [S3].

The bill bars claims against state agencies carrying out federally mandated or funded regulatory programs and instead routes them to the federal agency, and it excludes civil rights laws from its scope only by a separate construction rule — raising concerns that regulatory accountability would shift upward and become costlier [S3].
The bill sets no overall funding ceiling, so liability estimates in each agency's own impact analysis — not Congress — would determine the ultimate taxpayer cost [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real grievance here: a small landowner whose property value is essentially wiped out by a habitat or wetlands restriction currently bears a public burden alone, and the bill's appeal rights, data-access rules, and one-court jurisdiction address that fairly. But the compensation mechanism is built to scale with the size of the affected estate, so the money would flow overwhelmingly to large holdings, financed by agencies whose budgets would then shrink — meaning the same environmental rules would be enforced less. The procedural protections could have been enacted without the open-ended payment obligation; as written, the bill's cost to the public was potentially very large and essentially uncapped.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate's general calendar, but no committee took it up and the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Orrin Hatch introduced the Omnibus Property Rights Act of 1996 on July 16, 1996, with 26 senators originally joining [S1, S3, S5].
The bill attracted 34 cosponsors — 33 Republicans and one Democrat, Howell Heflin of Alabama [S4].
On July 17, 1996, it was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 498 [S3, S5].
No committee action, floor debate, or vote followed; the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died on the calendar [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and the public treasury were spared an open-ended new compensation liability, and existing endangered species and wetlands protections remained enforceable without a payer's veto. Large landowners and developers did not get the new compensation entitlement they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies, taxpayers, and existing environmental protections

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 16, 1996 and delivered introductory remarks; it never advanced past the Senate calendar.

for.name: Sen. Trent Lott and 33 other cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senate Majority Leader Lott; no cosponsor moved it to a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican — 33 of the 34 cosponsors were Republicans, with only Democrat Howell Heflin of Alabama joining — and the bill drew no recorded floor action or vote in either direction.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large landholders
industries.note: The 50% value-loss compensation trigger and binding arbitration would create a taxpayer-funded payout for large tracts constrained by habitat or wetlands rules. The cost of those payouts, and the deterred enforcement, would fall on the public.

industries.industry: Timber, agriculture, mining, and oil and gas interests
industries.note: Resource users facing species or wetland restrictions on their land would gain compensation rights and administrative appeals, making restrictions on extraction and development more expensive for the government to impose.
Ordinary owners whose land value collapses under a federal restriction would get a clear path to compensation, appeal rights, and attorney fees — the bill's most broadly shared benefit.

Agencies would pay compensation out of their own operating budgets and would face new paperwork, consent, and data-sharing requirements, shrinking funds available for enforcement that protects the public.
